Axios PM
By Mike Allen · Aug 24, 2026

☕️ Good Monday afternoon. Today's newsletter, edited by Alex Fitzpatrick, is 669 words, a 2½-min. read. Thanks to Sheryl Miller for copy editing.

🚨 Breaking: The USS Abraham Lincoln is headed for port in Thailand in early September after a record-breaking 250+ days at sea, USA Today reports.

 
 
1 big thing: Smarter ways to cool
 
Illustration: Shoshana Gordon/Axios

Engineers are looking for new ways to keep buildings cool without driving up electricity demand, Axios' Rebecca Falconer reports.

  • It's not just about generating more electricity to power air conditioners — it's how to use less power and ease demand when grids are most strained.

🏢 Some of the coolest new building tech includes smart windows and shading to block heat, reflective roof coatings, built-in energy storage to ease peak demand, and automation and ventilation to cut down on AC use.

Zoom in: In Colorado, clean-energy nonprofit RMI and Boulder County are testing passive daytime radiative cooling paint on roofs.

  • Ankit Kalanki, RMI's lead cooling expert, calls it "a more advanced version" of white paint — it reflects sunlight while also radiating heat into the sky.

Mat Santamouris, a University of New South Wales professor, tells Axios that the right mix of cooling methods for any particular building depends on its type, location and the local climate.

  • A 2024 study co-authored by Santamouris found that combining cool materials and greenery in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, could reduce peak ambient temperatures by up to 4.5°C. (Read the paper.)

🥵 Reality check: None of these technologies eliminates the need for AC.

  • Instead, the goal is to reduce how frequently and intensely it operates. Kalanki says: "Efficiency is the cheapest resource that we have available."

2. ⛽️ Diesel dilemma
 
Data: NYMEX, FactSet. (Continuous contract futures prices on U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude oil and New York Harbor ultra-low sulfur diesel.) Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Diesel futures prices have soared to roughly $100 above those of crude oil, Axios' Matt Phillips reports.

  • Their divergence reflects a dearth of global diesel refinery capacity.

💥 That shortage has been a growing issue since Ukraine launched a highly effective drone campaign targeting Russian refineries.

  • The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has also curtailed global supplies of refined products previously exported by Gulf states.

What's next: Costlier diesel will likely filter down to everyday life.

  • Diesel accounts for 3–5% of production costs for major crops like wheat, soybeans and corn.
  • Diesel is the key fuel for trucking, and its surge has already raised the costs of truck transportation for goods throughout the economy.

3. ⚡️ Catch me up
 
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent at a press conference today in Washington, D.C. Photo: Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
  1. 🇮🇷 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Operation Economic Outcast: The U.S. will impose punishing sanctions on countries and entities that do business with Iran — an attempt to bring the country to heel absent renewed military strikes. More from Barak Ravid.
  2. 📰 An independent arbitrator ruled that former Washington Post columnist Karen Attiah was wrongfully terminated last year over social posts tied to the death of Charlie Kirk, and ordered her reinstated with back pay and lost benefits. More from Sara Fischer.

Their ridiculously high tariffs on our Farmers and farm products has made life impossible for these great American Patriots, and has long created a 60 Billion Dollar Deficit between our two Countries." 4. 🐦 1 fun thing: Texting for the birds
 
Illustration: Natalie Peeples/Axios

A pair of new apps let users send messages at the speed of a carrier pigeon — or a snail or penguin, The New York Times reports.

  • Carrier Pidge and Roost are meant to evoke the slower, riskier messaging styles of yesteryear.

🪦 Plot twist: On Carrier Pidge, the digital pigeons sometimes get lost or die en route, just like their physical counterparts.

  • User Olivia Macdonald tells The Times: "The uncertainty of that, compared to the numbness that we feel receiving so many texts and notifications a day, is something that I just find really attractive about it."
